cases.summary: Large community lease. Two removal rights hide in the entry-purpose list, a rekey-on-default remedy hides in the default section, plus force majeure and a crime-only disclaimer.
Townhome community lease: 'as is' with no repair duty, 75-day move-out notice, a fee carve-out for any personal-injury claim, and a utility clause 'as permitted by law'.
Month-to-month duplex with addenda. Termination notice 'by the 15th' (about 15 days), a 35-day claim deadline in the deposit addendum, and a disclosure without the statutory notice.
Scanned condo lease. Two-business-day pay-or-quit, repair entry from 7:00 a.m., and a release from all claims buried in an indemnity paragraph; the U.S. flag is expressly allowed.

findings.title: Limit on landlord liability
findings.problem: The lease excuses the landlord's performance after events beyond its control. That isn't a release of liability by itself, but if it's used to skip duties Florida says can't be waived (like maintenance under s. 83.51), it would be void. A person should check.

span.quote: Management will not be in default of this Lease, and its obligations will be suspended, while performance is prevented by hurricane, flood, fire, pandemic, governmental order, labor dispute or other causes beyond Management's reasonable control.

findings.suggestedFix: Add: Nothing in this clause excuses Landlord's obligations under Part II of Chapter 83, Florida Statutes.

findings.title: Lockout
findings.problem: The lease allows the landlord to change the locks or otherwise keep the tenant out. Florida prohibits self-help lockouts; only a court eviction can remove a tenant.

span.quote: If Resident's right of occupancy is terminated for default, Management may file an eviction action, and upon termination of Resident's right of occupancy for default Management may change or rekey the locks to the Apartment Home.

findings.suggestedFix: Delete the clause. Landlord may recover possession only through a court eviction.

findings.title: Notice before the end of a fixed term
findings.problem: The lease requires 75 days' notice from the tenant before the term ends. Florida allows only 30 to 60 days.

span.quote: Tenant must give Landlord written notice of intent to vacate at least seventy-five (75) days before the end of the Lease term.

findings.suggestedFix: Either party must give written notice at least 30 days (and no more than 60 days) before the end of the lease term if they do not intend to renew.

findings.title: Waiver of landlord's maintenance duties
findings.problem: The lease shifts the landlord's code, structural or plumbing duties to the tenant. For a unit that is not a single-family home or duplex, these duties can't be waived.

span.quote: Except as expressly provided in this Lease, Landlord will not be required to make any repairs to the Townhome.

findings.suggestedFix: Landlord will comply with applicable building, housing, and health codes and keep the structural components and plumbing in good repair as required by s. 83.51(1), Florida Statutes.

findings.title: Waiver of attorney fees
findings.problem: The lease waives or limits the tenant's right to recover attorney fees. Florida says this right can't be waived in a lease.

span.quote: The prevailing party in any action arising under this Lease may recover reasonable attorney fees; however, no attorney fees may be recovered by either party in any claim for personal injury.

findings.suggestedFix: In any action to enforce this lease or Part II of Chapter 83, the prevailing party may recover reasonable attorney fees and court costs.

findings.title: Utility shutoff
findings.problem: The lease lets the landlord cut off a utility "according to statute" or as the law permits, without saying when. Florida bars landlord-caused utility interruptions, so a person should check what this clause is meant to allow.

span.quote: Landlord may suspend utility services furnished by Landlord only as permitted by applicable law.

findings.suggestedFix: Name the specific lawful circumstance, or delete the clause.
